title: Add Two Numbers
description: Brute force to optimized: reconstructing full numeric values (risking overflow) versus digit-by-digit column addition with a running carry.

blocks.text: You are given two non-empty linked lists, l1 and l2, representing two non-negative integers. Each node contains a single digit, and the digits are stored in REVERSE ORDER (least significant digit first). Add the two numbers and return the sum as a linked list, in the same reverse-order format.

blocks.caption: Add digit by digit, exactly like manual column addition, carrying over any overflow past 9

blocks.text: Given two numbers represented as linked lists of digits (least significant first), add them together and return the result in the same format.

blocks.title: Analogy: Adding Two Numbers by Hand, Column by Column
blocks.text: Like adding two numbers by hand on paper, starting from the rightmost (ones) column and working leftward, writing down each column's result digit and carrying over any extra amount into the next column to the left. Since the digits here are conveniently already stored in that exact right-to-left order, no reversing or extra bookkeeping about digit positions is needed at all.

blocks.caption: Each column's sum splits into a kept digit and a carry passed to the next column

Column 3: 3+4+1(carry)=8, no carry","Result digits: 7, 0, 8","342 + 465 = 807, matching digit by digit"],["Answer","[7,0,8]","Representing 807 in the same reverse-digit format"]]}

blocks.text: Before converting both linked lists into actual integers (which risks overflow for very large numbers) and converting the sum back, notice that the digits can be added directly, column by column, exactly like manual addition.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Since digits are stored least-significant-first, walking both lists simultaneously from their heads processes columns in exactly the right order for manual addition (rightmost first).

Observation 2: At each column, the digit contributed by each list (or 0, if that list has already run out) plus any carry from the previous column gives the column's total.

Observation 3: That total splits into a kept digit (total % 10) and a carry passed to the next column (total // 10), exactly matching how manual column addition works.

Observation 4: The process continues as long as EITHER list still has digits remaining, OR there's a leftover carry to account for, correctly handling lists of different lengths and a possible extra final digit.

Recognizing that walking both lists in lockstep, treating a shorter list as contributing 0 once exhausted, directly mirrors manual column addition and avoids any risk of numeric overflow from converting to native integers.
This is a direct simulation of manual column addition, digit by digit, using a running carry variable, entirely avoiding any conversion to native integer types.
Convert both linked lists into actual numeric values, add them using native arithmetic, then convert the sum back into a linked list of digits.

items: Walk each list, reconstructing its represented number using increasing place values (since digits are stored least-significant-first).
Add the two reconstructed numbers using native arithmetic, then peel off digits from the sum (least-significant-first) to build the result list.

codes.python:
def add_two_numbers(l1, l2):
    def to_number(node):
        digits = []
        while node:
            digits.append(str(node.val))                                   # collect digits, least significant first
            node = node.next
        return int("".join(reversed(digits)))                              # reverse to read most-significant-first, then parse

    total = to_number(l1) + to_number(l2)
    digits = [int(d) for d in str(total)][::-1]                            # convert back to a list of digits, least significant first
    dummy = ListNode(0)
    cur = dummy
    for d in digits:
        cur.next = ListNode(d)
        cur = cur.next
    return dummy.next


if __name__ == "__main__":
    l1 = ListNode(2, ListNode(4, ListNode(3)))
    l2 = ListNode(5, ListNode(6, ListNode(4)))
    result = add_two_numbers(l1, l2)
    values = []
    while result:
        values.append(result.val)
        result = result.next
    print(values)

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Reconstructing each number uses an increasing place-value multiplier, correctly matching the least-significant-first storage order.
Native addition handles the actual summing, though this risks overflow for very large inputs (up to 100 digits each, far exceeding standard integer types' safe range).
The sum is peeled apart digit by digit using modulo and integer division, naturally producing digits in the correct least-significant-first order for the result list.

blocks.text: The numbers are correctly reconstructed and added, so the result is accurate for inputs within the numeric type's safe range.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(m + n), where m and n are the lengths of the two lists.
Space: O(max(m, n)) for the resulting list.

Limitation: reconstructing full numeric values risks OVERFLOW for large inputs (up to 100 digits each, far beyond what standard integer or even long types can safely represent), a correctness risk that digit-by-digit addition avoids entirely.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force risks overflow by reconstructing full numeric values. Instead, simulate manual column addition directly: walk both lists simultaneously, treating a run-out list as contributing 0. At each step, sum both current digits plus any carry, split the total into a kept digit (total % 10) and a new carry (total // 10), and append the kept digit to the result. Continue as long as either list has remaining digits or a carry still needs propagating.

Use a dummy head and a cur pointer for the result. Maintain a carry variable, starting at 0. While l1, l2, or carry remain non-empty/non-zero: compute each list's current digit (or 0, if exhausted), sum them with the carry, update carry to the new overflow, and append the kept digit to the result. Advance whichever lists still have remaining nodes. Return dummy.next.
Simulate manual column addition directly on the linked lists, digit by digit, with a running carry.

blocks.title: Final answer
blocks.text: The result digits, in order, are [7,0,8], matching the expected sum (807).

codes.python:
def add_two_numbers(l1, l2):
    dummy = ListNode(0)
    cur = dummy
    carry = 0
    while l1 or l2 or carry:
        digit1 = l1.val if l1 else 0                                       # treat a run-out list as contributing 0 from here on
        digit2 = l2.val if l2 else 0
        total = digit1 + digit2 + carry
        carry = total // 10                                                # anything beyond a single digit becomes the next column's carry
        cur.next = ListNode(total % 10)
        cur = cur.next
        if l1:
            l1 = l1.next
        if l2:
            l2 = l2.next
    return dummy.next


if __name__ == "__main__":
    l1 = ListNode(2, ListNode(4, ListNode(3)))
    l2 = ListNode(5, ListNode(6, ListNode(4)))
    result = add_two_numbers(l1, l2)
    values = []
    while result:
        values.append(result.val)
        result = result.next
    print(values)

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(max(m, n)), a single combined pass through both lists.
Space: O(max(m, n)) for the resulting list (O(1) extra beyond the output itself).

This directly mirrors manual column addition: at every position, the two input digits (or 0, for an exhausted list) plus the incoming carry form that column's total; splitting this total into a units digit and a tens-place carry is exactly how addition naturally handles overflow past 9, at every scale, without ever needing to represent the full numbers as single native values.

blocks.text: Simulating manual column addition directly, digit by digit with a running carry, is both correct and overflow-safe for arbitrarily large numbers, unlike converting to native integer types first.

items: Converting to actual integers first, which can silently overflow (or require special big-integer handling) for inputs with many digits.
Forgetting the final leftover carry, which can produce a result missing its final (most significant) digit when the sum has one more digit than either input.
Not handling lists of different lengths correctly, forgetting to treat an exhausted list as simply contributing 0 rather than stopping the loop early.

items: Explicitly connect the algorithm to manual column addition (carrying digits, right to left), since framing it this way makes the carry-handling logic feel natural and easy to verify, rather than an arbitrary set of arithmetic rules.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Add two numbers represented as linked lists (digit by digit, least-significant-first)" points toward simulating manual column addition directly with a running carry, avoiding any native-integer conversion.

items: How would this change if the digits were stored MOST-significant-first instead? The lists would need to be reversed first (or processed via recursion using the call stack to reach the end first), since manual addition still needs to start from the least significant end.

How would you add more than 2 numbers at once? The same technique generalizes directly: sum every list's current digit plus the carry at each step, though tracking multiple list pointers simultaneously.

What if negative numbers needed to be supported? This would require tracking a sign separately and implementing subtraction logic (borrowing instead of carrying) when the signs differ, a substantially more involved extension.
The classic digit-by-digit column addition simulation, a technique broadly reusable for any problem requiring arbitrary-precision arithmetic without relying on native integer types.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(m + n) time, O(max(m, n)) space (with overflow risk for large inputs).
Optimized (digit-by-digit column addition): O(max(m, n)) time, O(max(m, n)) space.
